title: 1.8: You and I and the Personal Pronouns
author: Steven Brehe

lines.192: Have we got a chapter for you. We’ve seen that nouns can be the simple subjects in sentences. There is another kind of word that can be a simple subject (and can play other roles in a sentence). It’s the pronoun: a word that takes the place of a noun that appeared earlier in the context.
lines.194: Common English pronouns include I, me, mine, you, yours, he, she, it, him, her, his, hers, and others.
lines.195: When a pronoun takes the place of a noun, the noun replaced is called the antecedent of the pronoun. The antecedent usually appears before (ante-) its pronoun.
lines.197: In the sentences that follow, the pronouns are underlined. Not all of them are subjects:
lines.203: George loves Ethel. He loves her.
lines.205: (George is the antecedent of He, and Ethel is the antecedent of her.)
lines.207: Pearl painted Mr. Morton’s porch. She painted his porch.
lines.208: (Pearl is the antecedent of She, and Mr. Morton is the
lines.210: antecedent of his.) She enjoyed painting it.
lines.212: (Porch is the antecedent of it.) THE PERSONAL PRONOUNS
lines.214: There are thousands of nouns in English but only a few dozen pronouns, and those we use most are called the personal pronouns. All of the pronouns in the sentences above, and all that we discuss in this chapter, are personal pronouns.
lines.215: The following tables contain all of the personal pronouns in English, organized according to their several characteristics:
lines.219: First Person Second Person Third Person
lines.239: Notice that the third-person singular pronouns also have gender: he, she, or it.
lines.243: First Person Second Person Third Person
lines.247: we us you you they them
lines.250: our, ours your, yours their, theirs
lines.252: Notice that the possessive pronouns like yours, hers, and theirs don’t contain apostrophes. The tables also show us that all personal pronouns are classified by number, singular or plural.
lines.256: All personal pronouns are also classified by person. If you’re referring to yourself with pronouns, you use first-person pronouns: I, me, my, and mine, or the plural forms we, us, our(s).
lines.257: If you’re referring to the person you’re speaking with, you use second-person pronouns: you and your(s). The plural forms are the same.
lines.259: If you’re referring to another person outside the conversation, you use third-person pronouns:
lines.263: his, her, its (or the plurals they, them, their, and theirs)
lines.265: The third-person singular pronouns are also classified by gender: masculine (he, him, his), feminine (she, her, hers), and neuter (it, its).
lines.268: Finally, we classify personal pronouns by cases: the nominative case, the possessive case, and the objective case. These terms are used all the time in discussions of language, so it’s helpful to understand them. They refer to the forms of the pronouns that we use in certain positions in a sentence.
lines.270: The pronouns in the nominative case are the ones we use as subjects:
lines.272: I talked to Mr. Morton. You talked to Mr. Morton.
lines.276: They talked to Mr. Morton, too, but he is still juggling vases.
lines.278: The pronouns in the possessive case are used to indicate possession, and most of the possessive pronouns have two forms:
lines.280: Hey, that’s my vase. Hey, that’s your vase. Hey, that’s his vase. Hey, that’s her vase. Hey, that’s our vase. Hey, that’s their vase.
lines.281: (Or, That vase is mine.) (Or, That vase is yours.) (That vase is his.)
lines.282: (Or, That vase is hers.) (Or, That vase is ours.) (Or, That vase is theirs.)
lines.284: Notice that there are no apostrophes in these –s possessives, or in its. This frequently confuses inexperienced writers. Apostrophes show possession only with nouns: yours, ours, theirs, but children’s, women’s, Ruthie’s, Pearl’s, Mr. Morton’s.
lines.285: The pronouns in the objective case are used for almost every other purpose in a sentence. For example, when pronouns are the objects of prepositions, they are always in the objective case:
lines.287: I gave the book to Julie. I gave it to her. Mike said that I can ride with him. Give the vase to me.
lines.291: If we’re native speakers of English, we typically use the correct cases naturally. What we may have trouble remembering, as students of grammar, are terms for the three cases and the forms they describe. If you need to, you can learn this simple test sentence to help you remember the terms for the three cases of pronouns:
lines.293: N took O to P’s house.
lines.294: Here, obviously, N, O, and P stand for the three cases: nominative, objective, and possessive. Insert the right pronoun in each position, and you will know the case of the pronouns in question:
lines.296: He took her to their house. They took us to her house. We took them to his house.
lines.298: In each case, the first pronoun is nominative, the second objective, and the third possessive.
lines.300: The personal pronouns are the most important pronouns in English. We’ll examine other kinds later.
lines.303: Because we’re learning about the matter of person in this chapter, it seems like a good time to return to verbs briefly, and to one in particular.
lines.305: The verb to be is the most frequently used verb in English, and it’s also the most irregular verb. Because its irregular forms are tied up with the matter of person, we’ll examine be in detail here.
lines.307: These are the simple tenses of be. Notice how the forms change in the first, second, and third person, as well as in the singular and plural:
lines.314: I am You are He is
lines.318: I was You were He was
lines.322: I will be You will be He will be
lines.330: We are You are They are
lines.334: We were You were They were
lines.338: We will be You will be They will be
lines.339: Notice that the second-person forms are identical in the singular and plural. Notice, too, that there is great variety in the singular tenses, which use six different forms (am, are, is, was, were, and be), but the plurals are more consistent.
lines.341: As we move from the simple tenses to the tenses that require more auxiliaries, there is less variation in be. For that reason, we’ll look only at the singular in the following tenses.
lines.343: These are the perfect tenses of be:
lines.352: You have been She has been
lines.356: I had been You had been he had been
lines.360: I will have been You will have been She will have been
lines.362: In the perfect tense, the main verb is always the past participle, been, and the auxiliaries have, had, and has show tense and number in every tense but the future.
lines.364: These are the progressive tenses of be:
lines.372: I am being You are being He is being
lines.376: I was being You were being He was being
lines.379: I will be being You will be being He will be being
lines.381: Notice here and in the perfect progressive tense (which is below) that the main verb is always being. But the first auxiliary verb in these tenses show considerable variation: am, are, is, was, and were.

lines.412: 1. Use objective case pronouns as objects of prepositions.
lines.414: Sometimes you see nominative case pronouns used as objects of the prepositions:
lines.416: WRONG: Between Bob and I, we’ll get the job done. WRONG: Give the responsibility to Susan and I.
lines.418: But the nominative case is never right in this position. Always use the objective case as the object of the preposition:
lines.419: Between Bob and me, we’ll get the job done. Give the report to Susan and me.
lines.421: In the second example, you can make certain that you have the right pronoun by leaving out Susan: Give the report to me. If me is right in that sentence, it’s also right when used in to Susan and me.
lines.425: In both sentences, plural pronouns like us could also work in place of the two objects, but the pronouns must still be in the objective case.
lines.426: By the way, there is no grammatical reason to put me last in the two examples above; it’s a matter of courtesy. And courtesy is important, too.
lines.430: The third-person singular pronouns (he, she, it, and the others) can be troublesome. Consider this passage:
lines.432: Each physician should submit his credentials to the hospital’s human resources department. Each nurse must submit her credentials, too.
lines.433: In the past, these sentences may have been completely acceptable to most readers and editors. As you know, they are not acceptable today. Most readers and editors object to the apparent assumption that all physicians are men and all nurses are women.
lines.435: Today the usual way to avoid this problem, and the way we recommend in most cases, is to make the sentence plural:
lines.437: All physicians and nurses must submit their credentials to the hospital’s human resources department.
lines.438: Sometimes we can omit pronouns altogether:
lines.439: All physicians and nurses must submit credentials . . . .
lines.441: Other ways, like the use of his or her or his/her, are possible, but some editors regard them as awkward or wordy.
lines.443: There’s still another way. Today they, them, and their are sometimes used as singular pronouns, when you don’t know the gender of the antecedent:
lines.445: Tell your doctor to send me their diagnosis of your case.
lines.446: Some people approve, and some don’t, so (in certain professional contexts) tread carefully and consider the context. Again, you can rewrite the sentence to sidestep the entire issue: Send me the diagnosis . . . .
lines.450: Used carelessly, pronouns can be confusing.
lines.452: CONFUSING: The speaker discussed the causes of the recession, but I didn’t understand it at all.
lines.454: BETTER: In his speech, the speaker discussed the causes of the recession, but I didn’t understand him at all.
lines.455: BETTER: The speaker discussed the causes of the recession in his speech, but I didn’t understand it at all.
lines.457: These three sentences demonstrate the importance of selecting the right pronouns for your context. This is called pronoun agreement. When writers neglect pronoun agreement, they often confuse their readers.
lines.459: Here are two more examples of pronoun ambiguity. In these sentences, what is the antecedent of she?
lines.461: Sally’s mother has collected dolls since she was twelve years old.
lines.462: Sally told her mother that she was too old to play with dolls.
lines.464: The reader shouldn’t have to guess who she is. It’s usually easy to rewrite the sentences to avoid ambiguity:
lines.466: Sally’s mother has collected dolls for twenty-three years.
lines.468: Sally thought that her mother was too old to play with dolls and told her so.
lines.472: 4. Maintain a consistent point of view.
lines.474: That is, don’t change pronouns unnecessarily. Consider the confused point of view in this paragraph:
lines.475: When you have worked with adolescents for a few months, you will know what to expect. People who work with adolescents learn quickly what problems they will encounter in most situations. You get to know how they think.
lines.477: Don’t shift point of view without a good reason. Be consistent in your use of pronouns. Use third person or, when reasonable, first person, or a careful combination of first and third.
lines.479: Use second person (you) when it makes sense to address the reader directly.
lines.480: Here’s an improved version of the same paragraph:
lines.482: After you have worked with adolescents for a few months, you will know what to expect. You will quickly learn what problems you will encounter in most situations. You will get to know how they think.
lines.483: Inexperienced writers sometimes overuse the second-person pronouns , but it is usually acceptable in instructions like the passage above, or in personal communications like letters and emails. The second-person is also useful in establishing a more informal, conversational tone, as we have done in these chapters.
lines.485: It is also grammatical to use the indefinite pronoun one in passages like this:
lines.486: After one has worked with adolescents for a few months, one will know what to expect. One quickly learns what problems will be encountered in most situations.
lines.488: This use of one is now often seen as excessively formal and impersonal, and even awkward. Using you is usually a better idea.
lines.492: Using they, you, and it imprecisely is often a symptom of careless writing:
lines.494: WRONG: They don’t allow you to build fires in the city park.
lines.495: BETTER: The city doesn’t allow anyone to build fires in the city park.
lines.497: WRONG: It says in the letter that your band, Noise Pollution, is banned from performing in the city limits.
lines.499: BETTER: The City Council says in its letter that your band, Noise Pollution, is banned from performing in the city limits.
